facts.raw_span: A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest
the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier
then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom
He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes
Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation
A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness
Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity
Sinus rhythm at approximately 100 beats per minute
Right axis deviation
Prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1
No acute occlusions found
QT interval of 360 ms measurable in leads V4-V6

concepts.why: The patient's ECG findings, including right axis deviation, prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1, and a QT interval of 360 ms, are consistent with Brugada syndrome, which can cause cardiac arrest.

The patient's history of COPD and complaints of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation, as well as the family member's witness of him struggling for air, suggest a COPD exacerbation, which can lead to respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.

The patient's initial rhythm of pulseless electrical activity and subsequent sinus rhythm with a rate of approximately 100 beats per minute may be consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which can cause cardiac arrest.

The patient's complaints of shortness of breath and the family member's witness of him struggling for air, combined with the cardiac arrest, may suggest a pulmonary embolism, which can cause cardiac arrest.

The patient's ECG findings, including right axis deviation and prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1, may be consistent with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, which can cause cardiac arrest.
The absence of acute occlusions found in coronary angiography rules out acute coronary syndrome as the primary cause, but it is still a relevant consideration given the patient's presentation.
